newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland promises to protect Pope during visit.
newsitem.headline: Poland promises to protect Pope during visit.

text.p: Poland is taking all steps necessary to prevent threats to the Pope and disruption of his visit to his native country next month, Interior Minister Leszek Miller said on Monday.
Miller was asked to comment on press reports that Polish anarchist and homosexual groups had invited German counterparts to join them in protests against the May 31-June 10 Papal pilgrimage.

Lebanon said this month it had been warned through Interpol about a plan to assassinate the Pope during his trip there. His trip to Sarajevo in April was marred by the discovery before he arrived of anti-tank mines planted under a bridge on his route.

"We are very closely following all signals, whether from Lebanon, Italy, Sarajevo or Poland itself. We will use all methods, including preventive ones, to avert disruption of the Holy Father's visit by anyone," Miller told a news conference.

Poland's Rzeczpospolita daily reported on Monday that Polish security had information anarchists might be preparing protests during a Eucharistic Congress in the western city of Wroclaw, which the Pope will attend at the start of his trip.
Last year Berlin gays staged extravagant protests, dressing as punk altar boys or condoms, during the Pontiff's visit, against his conservative stance on artificial birth control and homosexuality.
Although around 90 percent of Poles are Roman Catholics, there are factions who say the Church has too much influence.

Some rightist radicals, calling for a settling of accounts for abuses before the 1989 fall of communism, have been disrupting appearances by ex-communists such as President Aleksander Kwasniewski, who will meet the Pope during the trip.
The head of Poland's Government Protection Office (BOR) has been replaced in the midst of planning for the Papal visit, after Polish rightists in Paris flung eggs at Kwasniewski.

Debate on such issues as abortion, recently liberalised despite Church protests, is an issue in campaigning for elections due around September in which the opposition, grouped around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union, hopes to supplant the current government led by ex-communists.
Miller, an ex-communist, said he hoped political tensions would ease during the trip, when about four million people are expected to attend gatherings to see the Pope.
"We hope it will contribute towards calming sometimes very excited emotions," he said.

Miller said a total of 33,000 police from around Poland would be drafted in for the trip around 12 Polish towns and cities, plus 5,000 professional and volunteer firemen, hundreds of security service agents and 1,000 interior ministry troops.
The Church is mobilising 35,000 marshals along the route.
Poland has spent more than $3 million before the trip on sophisticated equipment that can stop bombs being detonated remotely or test food instantly for safety.
